subcategory: Responsible AI, Human Rights and Safety
oneSentence: An approach to designing, using and governing AI so it is safe, fair, accountable and under appropriate human control.
plainExplanation:
Responsible AI is about using AI in ways that reduce harm and support people’s rights, safety and dignity. It asks practical questions before and during use: Who could be helped? Who could be harmed? Who is accountable if something goes wrong? What must stay a human judgement?

What goes in includes the purpose of the system, the data used, the people affected, the rules around it and the context where it will be used. Then organisations test, document and monitor the system. They look for problems such as unfair treatment, privacy risks, security weaknesses, poor performance and over-reliance by staff.

What happens next is not just technical. Teams set limits, add human oversight, create ways to challenge results and decide when AI should not be used at all. A guardrail is a rule or design feature that restricts unsafe or inappropriate behaviour.

What comes out should be more than a working tool. It should be a system with clear responsibility, checks, records and a way to fix harm. Responsible AI is often confused with AI ethics, which is the wider discussion of values and principles, and with AI safety, which often focuses more narrowly on preventing harmful failures.

everydayAnalogy.title: Using a document-matching tool in an office
everydayAnalogy.story: A clerk receives 200 photographed forms from clinics in different regions and uses software to match each photo to the right template. Before trusting it, the office checks whether the software works equally well on crumpled pages, low light images and forms in different languages. They set a rule that uncertain matches must go to a human reviewer, and they keep a record of errors so the process can improve. They also decide the tool may suggest a template, but it may not reject an application on its own.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: This analogy uses a narrow office task with a clear right answer, so it can make responsible AI look simpler than it often is. Many real AI systems affect people in less visible ways, use more complex data and create harms that are harder to detect than a wrong template match. Responsible AI also includes governance, accountability, privacy, labour and human rights questions that go beyond checking accuracy.

visual.title: How responsible AI is applied
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to describe responsible AI as an ongoing process: define purpose, test risks, set human controls, and monitor after deployment.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with four connected boxes. Each box names one stage in applying responsible AI, from planning to ongoing monitoring. Read in order. Under each box, a short caption states what teams check or decide at that stage.

steps.label: 1. Define the use
steps.explanation: State the task, the expected benefit, the people affected and the context. Ask whether AI is appropriate for this use at all.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rectangle labelled 'Define the use' with small icons for goal, people and context beneath the title.

steps.label: 2. Check risks and data
steps.explanation: Review the data, likely failure points, fairness concerns, privacy issues, security risks and possible human rights impacts.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second rectangle connected by an arrow. Add a checklist icon and small tags reading 'data', 'fairness', 'privacy', 'security'.

steps.label: 3. Add controls
steps.explanation: Set guardrails, assign accountability, require human review where needed and record how the system should and should not be used.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third rectangle with icons for a shield, a person reviewing, and a document log.

steps.label: 4. Monitor and improve
steps.explanation: Track performance, complaints and unexpected harms after deployment, then update, limit or stop the system if needed.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth rectangle with icons for a dashboard, alert symbol and repair tool. Use a feedback arrow from step 4 back to step 2.

visual.interaction: On hover or keyboard focus, each step reveals one example question, such as 'Who could be harmed?' or 'What must stay a human decision?'
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram shows four stages in a continuous responsible AI process. First, define the use: what the system will do, why it is needed, who is affected and whether AI should be used. Second, check risks and data: examine data quality, possible unfair effects, privacy and security risks, and broader human rights impacts. Third, add controls: set limits, assign accountability, require human review for suitable cases and document proper use. Fourth, monitor and improve: watch for errors, complaints and new harms after deployment, and then adjust, restrict or stop the system if needed. A feedback arrow from the last stage back to risk checking shows this is ongoing, not one-time.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-step horizontal diagram with a feedback arrow from the final box back to the second box, showing that monitoring leads to renewed risk checks.

workedExample.scenario: A city archives team wants AI to sort scanned permit forms into five template types before staff review them.
workedExample.input: 5,000 past form images with the correct template label, plus a rule that any prediction below 85% confidence goes to a human checker.
process: The team tests the system on new images, including blurred photos and forms from older mobile phones.
They find overall accuracy is 93%, but one template drops to 78% when images are dim.
They decide the tool may only suggest a template and must send low-confidence or dim-image cases to staff.
They log errors weekly and retrain only after checking whether changes improve weak cases without creating new problems.
workedExample.result: The team saves time on routine sorting, but keeps human review for uncertain cases and avoids using the tool as the final decision-maker.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office considers an AI tool to draft a situation report from approved, non-sensitive source material and staff notes.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Responsible AI helps the office decide what sources are allowed, what checks are needed, who approves the draft and when human judgement must override the tool.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste confidential, protection-sensitive, personal, security-sensitive or operational information into an unapproved public AI service. A human reviewer must verify the draft, its sourcing and any sensitive implications before sharing.

whyItMatters: Responsible AI affects whether a tool saves time safely or creates unfair, unsafe or unaccountable outcomes. For non-specialists, it helps frame better questions before adoption: Is this use appropriate? Who might be harmed? What evidence supports it? Who checks the output? What happens when it fails? These questions improve procurement, policy, leadership decisions and day-to-day use.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an AI system is accurate, it is responsible.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Accuracy matters, but it is only one part. A system can score well on average and still be unfair to some groups, expose private data, fail in unusual conditions or be used without clear accountability. Responsible AI asks about the whole system around the model, not just one performance number.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Responsible AI only matters for high-risk tools used by governments or large companies.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The stakes differ by context, but even small or routine tools can cause real harm if people rely on them too much, if access is unequal or if mistakes are hard to correct. The level of control should match the risk, yet basic checks and accountability still matter for simpler uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding a human in the loop automatically makes AI responsible.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Human involvement helps only if it is meaningful. If staff are rushed, poorly informed or expected to approve machine outputs without question, human review may be superficial. Responsible AI requires clear authority, time, information and the option to disagree with the system.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Responsible AI means using AI with safeguards so people are treated fairly, risks are checked, and humans remain accountable for important outcomes.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Responsible AI is an organisational approach for the full AI lifecycle: problem definition, data selection, model development, evaluation, deployment and post-deployment monitoring. It combines governance and technical controls to manage risks such as discrimination, privacy intrusion, security failures, unsafe behaviour, opacity, exclusion and over-automation. Typical mechanisms include impact assessments, documentation, testing across relevant groups and conditions, guardrails, incident reporting, human oversight, audit trails and routes for contesting harmful outcomes. The exact definition is not fully uniform across organisations, and some use 'trustworthy AI' to emphasise reliability and confidence, but the core idea is practical accountability for how AI affects people.

keyTakeaway: Responsible AI is not just building a useful system; it is making sure the system can be used safely, fairly and accountably in the real world.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits responsible AI?
options: Deploying a model because it scored highest on a benchmark test
Using AI to suggest outputs, while setting human review rules, checking risks and tracking harms after launch
Assuming the vendor is responsible for all problems because they built the model
Adding a warning label once and treating the job as finished
quickCheck.explanation: Responsible AI is an ongoing practice, not a one-time score or disclaimer. It includes risk checks, clear accountability, limits on use, suitable human oversight and monitoring after deployment.

contested: The broad direction is widely shared, but organisations do not define the term in exactly the same way. Some emphasise ethics, some governance, some safety, and some use 'trustworthy AI' as a near-synonym.
